essences_bois.intro: Not all woods burn the same. Knowing which to choose saves wood and energy.
etapes: To start: birch (its bark burns even when damp), spruce and pine twigs (resinous, they catch quickly), thin hazel.
To last and make embers: beech, oak, hornbeam and ash, hardwoods that burn long and give steady heat.
Avoid as logs: conifers (pine, spruce), which crackle, throw sparks and blacken pots; poplar, willow and alder, which burn too fast.
Recognising dry wood: it's light, rings clearly when you knock two pieces together, snaps cleanly, and the bark comes off easily.
Never burn yew, oleander, cherry laurel or treated or painted wood: their fumes are toxic.
attention: Always dead wood picked up from the ground or dry standing wood, never a living tree.
essences_bois.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten for Bivaska

contourner.titre: Getting round an obstacle without losing your bearing
contourner.intro: A marsh or a ravine in your way? With the compass and your steps, you can go round it and get back exactly on your bearing.
etapes: At the obstacle, turn 90° (to the right, for example) and walk, counting your steps, until you're past the obstacle.
Take up your original bearing again and walk until you're past the obstacle on the other side.
Turn 90° the other way (to the left) and walk the SAME number of steps as before.
Take up your original bearing again: you're back on your line of march.
Simpler when you can see far: pick a tree or rock on the other side of the obstacle, on your line, walk round to it and take a new bearing from there.
contourner.source: US Army map reading and land navigation manuals (public domain), rewritten for Bivaska

ps_garrot.intro: The life-saving action when a limb is bleeding heavily and pressure isn't enough, or when you need your hands free.
attention: A tourniquet hurts a lot: that's normal. Not tight enough, it makes the bleeding worse: tighten until it stops completely.
Never a tourniquet on the neck, chest or belly: there, pressure only.
isole: Take a band 4 to 5 cm wide: folded scarf, fabric belt, strap. Never a string or thin cord.
Place it 5 to 7 cm above the wound, between the wound and the heart, not on a joint.
Tie a knot, put a strong stick on it, tie another knot over the stick.
Twist the stick until the bleeding stops completely.
Lock the stick (slide it under a tie) so it doesn't unwind.
Write the time it was applied where it can be seen, on the tourniquet or on the skin.
Don't loosen it to “let the limb breathe”: it stays on until medical care takes over.
alerte: A tourniquet in place means urgent evacuation: do everything to get out or be found
ps_garrot.source: Written for Bivaska: manuals FM 4-25.11 and FM 21-76 (public domain), cross-checked with remote-area first-aid recommendations (WMS, ERC)

ps_plaie_soin.titre: Caring for a wound over several days
ps_plaie_soin.intro: Far from help, the danger of a wound is infection. Thorough cleaning is the most effective action.
attention: Before you go, check that your tetanus vaccination is up to date (booster every 10 years).
isole: Once the bleeding has stopped, rinse the wound with at least 1 litre of drinking water (boiled then cooled, or filtered), as a jet: bottle with a pierced cap or a pierced plastic bag that you squeeze.
Remove remaining dirt with disinfected tweezers.
Clean, tidy wound less than 6 hours old: bring the edges together with strips (adhesive sutures), without tightening.
Dirty wound, animal bite or older wound: don't close it. Leave it open under a clean dressing so it can drain.
Change the dressing every day, or as soon as it's wet or dirty, rinsing again.
Keep the area rested and raised if possible.
alerte: Red streak running towards the heart
ps_plaie_soin.source: Written for Bivaska: manuals FM 4-25.11 and FM 21-76 (public domain), cross-checked with remote-area first-aid recommendations (WMS, ERC)

ps_surveiller.intro: Without help, how the casualty's condition develops decides everything: stay, leave or do everything to signal. Taking notes lets you see it coming.
isole: At first every 15 minutes, then every hour, note in the notebook: the time, consciousness, breathing, pulse, skin, pain.
Consciousness: fully awake and coherent? Responds only to voice? Only when pinched? Doesn't respond?
Breathing: count the belly movements for 30 seconds and multiply by 2. Normal at rest: 12 to 20 per minute.
Pulse at the wrist (thumb side) or neck: count for 30 seconds and multiply by 2. Normal at rest: 60 to 100.
Skin: colour, temperature, sweating. Pale, cold and clammy: warning.
If they're conscious and have no belly injury, give them drinks regularly. Clear urine shows they're drinking enough.
Keep them dry, insulated from the ground, out of the wind, and change their position if they can't move by themselves.
alerte: Consciousness drops from one note to the next
Breathing over 30 or under 10 per minute
ps_surveiller.source: Written for Bivaska: manuals FM 4-25.11 and FM 21-76 (public domain), cross-checked with remote-area first-aid recommendations (WMS, ERC)

simple.intro: The basic knot, at the root of almost all the others. A quick stopper at the end of a rope or line.
etapes: Make a loop by crossing the working end over the standing part.
Pass the working end through the loop, going in from underneath.
Tighten by pulling both ends.
attention: It jams under a heavy load and weakens the rope. For a solid stopper, prefer the figure-eight.
simple.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

arret_double.intro: A bigger stopper than the overhand: it won't pull through an eyelet and is the basis of the double fisherman's knot.
etapes: Start like an overhand knot, without tightening.
Pass the working end through the loop a second time, in the same direction.
Tighten gently, guiding the two turns so they wrap side by side.
attention: Very hard to untie after a heavy load.
arret_double.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

plat_ganse.intro: The reef knot that comes undone in one pull, like a shoelace. Handy for closing a bag, rolling a tarp or tying up a pack.
etapes: Tie the first half of a reef knot: cross the left end over the right and tuck it under.
For the second half, fold one of the ends into a bight (a U-shaped loop).
This time cross the right end over the left and tie with the bight.
Tighten. To untie, just pull the free end of the bight.
attention: Like the reef knot, it is only for binding something: never for joining two ropes that will bear a load.
plat_ganse.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

chirurgien.intro: An improved reef knot: the first crossing is doubled and doesn't slip while you tie the second. Ideal for tightening a bandage, a bundle or fishing line.
etapes: Cross the two ends and wrap them twice around each other.
Pull to tighten this double crossing: it holds by itself.
Cross again, the other way, just once.
Tighten all four strands evenly.
chirurgien.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

huit_boucle.intro: A very strong fixed loop that is easy to check at a glance. For hanging a load, clipping onto a rope or tensioning a line.
etapes: Fold the rope to form a bight about 30 cm long.
With this doubled section, make a loop by crossing it over both strands.
Pass the bight behind both strands.
Bring it back through the loop from the front.
Tighten by pulling the loop one way and both strands the other. The strands must stay parallel, without crossing.
attention: Hard to untie after a big load. If the strands cross inside the knot, start again.
huit_boucle.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

huit_rengaine.intro: The same figure-eight loop, but tied around a tree, a ring or a harness that you can't thread into a loop already tied.
etapes: Tie a single figure-eight, without tightening it, about 1 m from the end.
Pass the working end around the tree or through the ring.
Feed it back into the eight where the working end of the first eight comes out.
Follow exactly the path of the first strand, in reverse, always staying on the same side of it.
Come out parallel to the standing part, tighten, and leave a tail of at least 10 cm.
huit_rengaine.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

papillon.intro: A fixed loop in the middle of a rope that takes a pull in three directions. For hanging gear on a taut line, or isolating a damaged section of rope.
etapes: In the middle of the rope, make a bight.
Twist this bight twice on itself, in the same direction: it forms an eight, with a small opening at the bottom.
Fold the top of the bight down, in front of the twists.
Pass it through the bottom opening, then pull it upwards.
Tighten by pulling the loop one way and the two strands in opposite directions.
attention: Check the shape: a loop coming out to the side, and the two strands coming out of the knot on opposite sides. If not, start again.
papillon.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

chaise_double.intro: Two fixed loops that don't slide, tied in the middle of a rope. They can serve as an improvised seat for hoisting or lowering someone.
etapes: Fold the rope in two to form a long bight.
With this doubled section, make a small loop as for a bowline.
Pass the bight up through the small loop from underneath.
Open the bight and pass it over the two big loops, until it encircles the knot from behind.
Tighten by pulling the two big loops one way and the standing part the other.
attention: To carry a person, first test the knot with your own weight, close to the ground.
chaise_double.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

vache.intro: The quickest way to fix a loop of rope or a sling around a branch, a post or a handle.
etapes: Fold the rope in two to form a bight.
Pass the bight around the branch or through the ring.
Pass both strands through the bight.
Pull both strands to tighten.
attention: It only holds well if both strands pull together. With only one strand loaded, it can slip.
vache.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

demi_cabestan.intro: A rope brake using a single carabiner: for lowering a load gently or belaying someone climbing.
etapes: Make two identical loops, side by side, in the rope.
Fold them against each other like closing a book, not one behind the other as for a clove hitch.
Clip the carabiner through both loops and lock the gate.
Always keep hold of the brake strand: your hand does the braking. The closer the brake strand is brought to the loaded strand, the less it brakes.
attention: Only with a locking carabiner, preferably pear-shaped.
It twists the rope. Abseiling without training is very dangerous: this hitch is mainly for lowering gear or belaying someone.
demi_cabestan.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

machard.intro: A friction hitch: it slides by hand and locks as soon as you pull down. For climbing a rope, tensioning a line or making a handle.
etapes: Take a loop of cord thinner than the main rope.
Wrap it 4 or 5 times around the rope going upwards, in tight turns that don't overlap.
Pass the bottom end through the top loop.
Pull this end down: the knot locks. To move it, push the turns by hand.
attention: It only locks in one direction, downwards. To lock both ways, use the Prusik knot.
machard.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

largage.intro: It holds a load and comes undone at once when you pull the free end, even from a distance. Handy for a hammock, a hanging bag or an animal.
etapes: Pass a bight of the working end behind the branch.
Form a bight in the part that will bear the load and pass it, from the front, through the first bight.
Pull the working end to tighten the first bight onto the second.
Form a bight with the working end and pass it through the second bight.
Pull the load-bearing part to lock everything. To release, pull the free end.
attention: Never for carrying a person: it can come undone with jerks.
largage.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

jambe_chien.intro: Shortens a rope without cutting it, or sets aside a damaged section until something better turns up.
etapes: Fold the rope into an S to form three parallel strands, the length to be removed. The damaged part should be in the middle strand.
At one end, make a loop in the single strand and slip it over the bight on that side.
Do the same at the other end.
Put the rope under tension: the knot holds as long as it's loaded.
attention: It comes undone if the rope slackens. For more security, lock each bight with a toggle or a whipping.
jambe_chien.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

ruban.intro: The only reliable knot for joining two flat slings, or closing a sling into a loop.
etapes: Tie a loose overhand knot at the end of one sling, nice and flat, without twists.
Feed the end of the other sling in where the first end comes out.
Follow exactly the path of the knot, in reverse, staying flat against the first sling.
Tighten very hard by pulling each strand, and leave tails of at least 7 cm.
attention: It can creep little by little with use: check the length of the tails before each use.
ruban.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

ancre.intro: Fixes a rope securely to a ring, an improvised anchor or a stone with a hole. It stands up well to jerks and water.
etapes: Make two round turns around the ring or branch.
Pass the working end around the standing part.
Tuck it under the two round turns.
Finish with a half hitch on the standing part and tighten.
ancre.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

brelage_diagonal.intro: Joins two poles that cross at an angle, or that tend to spring apart: for bracing a shelter frame or a tripod.
etapes: Tie a timber hitch around both poles, diagonally, at the crossing point.
Make 3 or 4 tight turns along the same diagonal.
Make 3 or 4 turns along the other diagonal.
Make 2 or 3 frapping turns between the two poles, around the previous turns.
Finish with a clove hitch on one of the poles.
attention: Only with dead wood, and dismantle everything before leaving.
brelage_diagonal.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

palomar.intro: The simplest hook knot and one of the strongest: useful for a survival fishing line.
etapes: Double about 15 cm of line and pass the loop through the eye of the hook.
Tie a loose overhand knot with the doubled line, the hook hanging below.
Pass the whole hook through the loop.
Wet the knot, tighten by pulling both strands, then trim the tail.
attention: Fishing is regulated: a licence is generally required, and the rules vary by country and waterway.
palomar.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

clinch.intro: The other great knot for a hook or lure, when the eye is too small for a doubled line.
etapes: Pass the end of the line through the eye.
Wrap the end 5 to 7 times around the main line.
Pass the end through the small loop that has formed near the eye.
Then pass it back through the big loop that has just formed.
Wet it and tighten gently, then trim the tail.
clinch.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

surliure.intro: Stops the end of a rope from fraying, using thin thread: string, dental floss or thick sewing thread.
etapes: Fold the thread into a bight and lay it along the rope, loop towards the end of the rope.
Wind the thread tightly around the rope and the bight, working towards the end, over a length of about 1.5 times the rope's diameter. Leave the loop sticking out.
Pass the end of the thread through the loop.
Pull the other end of the thread, the starting one, to draw the loop under the turns, as far as the middle.
Trim both ends flush.
attention: A synthetic rope can also be melted with a lighter, but a whipping holds better and doesn't cut your hands.
surliure.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

simple_ganse.intro: A temporary stopper or tie that comes undone at once when you pull the end.
etapes: Make a loop as for an overhand knot.
Instead of passing the end, pass a bight of the working end through the loop.
Tighten. To untie, pull the end of the bight.
simple_ganse.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

huit_ganse.intro: A figure-eight stopper that comes undone instantly: to lock a rope temporarily in an eyelet or a pulley.
etapes: Make a loop, then pass the working end behind the standing part, as for a figure-eight.
For the last pass through the loop, pass a bight of the working end instead of the end.
Tighten. To untie, pull the end of the bight.
huit_ganse.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

stevedore.intro: A figure-eight with one more turn: a bigger stopper that won't pull through a wide hole and is still easy to untie.
etapes: Make a loop by crossing the working end over the standing part.
Wrap the working end twice around the standing part, instead of once for the figure-eight.
Pass the working end through the starting loop.
Tighten by pulling both ends.
stevedore.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

pomme.intro: A ball of rope at the end of a cord, which adds weight for throwing it far: over a branch to hang a food bag, or to someone.
etapes: Wrap the rope 3 times around two fingers, leaving the standing part hanging.
Make 3 turns around the first ones, at right angles, tightening them in the middle.
Pass the end inside the first set of turns, then make 3 turns around the second set, passing inside the first each time.
Remove your fingers. Tighten little by little, following the rope in order, until you get a firm ball.
Tie the end to the standing part with two half hitches.
attention: Don't put a stone in the centre if it might be thrown towards a person: the ball becomes dangerous.
pomme.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

ecoute_double.intro: Joins two ropes of very different thickness, or wet and slippery ones. Safer than the single sheet bend.
etapes: Make a bight with the thicker rope.
Pass the end of the thinner rope up through the bight from underneath.
Take it behind both strands of the bight, then tuck it under itself.
Make a second turn in the same place, next to the first, and tuck that under itself too.
Tighten by pulling both ropes.
ecoute_double.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

carrick.intro: Joins two thick ropes that will bear a heavy load. It stays easy to untie, even after getting wet.
etapes: With the first rope, make a loop whose end passes over the standing part.
Lay the end of the second rope under this loop.
Work the second rope forward, alternating at each crossing: over the first rope's standing part, under its end, over the loop.
Keep alternating: under its own standing part, then over the loop. The two ends come out diagonally, on opposite sides.
Pull both ropes: the knot capsizes and settles. That's normal.
attention: Check that at each crossing the rope goes over once, under once. A single mistake and the knot fails.
carrick.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska
